claims.text: The existence and integrity of a native, adherent oxide layer governs whether Q235 steel maintains corrosion protection during room-temperature and high-temperature aggressive-salt exposure.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel is predominantly magnetite with minor hematite.
An intact native oxide film acts as a diffusion barrier that limits salt attack and oxygen ingress.
Removal, damage, or microcracking of the oxide film predisposes Q235 steel to accelerated oxidation and mass change.
As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin oxide film developed during ambient storage.
Gentle cleaning can preserve the native oxide layer, whereas mechanical polishing or mild acid etching can remove it.
The preserved-film and removed-film groups will receive identical annealing and aggressive-salt exposure treatments.
Aggressive-salt exposure will be conducted at 700–900 °C using a boiler-relevant salt such as Na2SO4-NaCl for 50–100 hours.
Room-temperature humid-environment tests will be used to contrast low-temperature corrosion behavior with high-temperature behavior.
At high temperature, a well-adherent oxide film reduces oxidation and surface degradation by restricting transport of aggressive species.
Thermal-stress-induced microcracking makes the substrate more accessible to aggressive salts.
At room temperature, the oxide film is less challenged than it is during high-temperature salt exposure.
Disruption of the oxide film at room temperature may lower surface hardness and compromise long-term stability.
Samples retaining the native oxide film will have lower mass-change rates than samples from which the film was removed.
Samples retaining the native oxide film will retain more surface hardness than samples from which the film was removed.
The protective difference between intact-film and removed-film samples will be clear at 700–900 °C but less pronounced under room-temperature humid conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when substantial alloying additions, contaminants, or coatings alter the surface-oxide chemistry.
The magnetite-to-hematite ratio, minor impurities, and salt chemistry may alter the oxide film's barrier effectiveness.

At 750 °C for 75 hours, the governing role of the native film will be rejected if preserved-film and removed-film samples show no statistically significant differences in mass change, hardness retention, or oxide integrity.
